items.name: Readability
items.evidence: Business logic uses single-letter names (`a`, `b`, `n`, `s`, `t`, `k`), which triggers the cap. The `#if 0` / `""" "` / `" """` switching trick has no comment in the file. The limb layout does have a short comment.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: There are no functions: Python is top-level script code and all the C logic sits in one main(). The hand-rolled bignum adds complexity the task didn't ask for. The `hasattr(sys, "set_int_max_str_digits")` guard is unnecessary on Python 3.12.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: Python does no argument validation (`n = int(sys.argv[1])`). C calls `strtol(argv[1], NULL, 10)` without checking endptr or errno. `n / 43` is a magic constant. The calloc result is checked.

items.name: Boundary and large inputs
items.evidence: f(0), f(1) and large n are exact in both languages. But Python with a negative n prints 0 and exits 0. Missing or invalid input only fails through an uncaught traceback. In C, a non-numeric argument makes strtol return 0, so it prints 0 and exits 0.

items.name: Exact invocation contract
items.evidence: Works with plain `gcc main.py.c -o cmain` (no warnings even with -Wall -Wextra) and with `python3 main.py.c N`. Each run prints only the number. The hidden test passed.
